When you get to the core of it disputing man made climate change is either disputing the fact that we are putting greenhouse gasses into the air, or you are disputing the fact that greenhouse gasses heat the atmosphere. There is some question to how much warming these gasses account for compared to natural cycles, but even that gets blown out of proportion by climate change deniers (I'm assuming you given the name of the subverse).

For example: "blah blah blah, there are natural warming and cooling cycles, we're going into a warming cycle, blah blah blah." This argument fails to take into account cause and effect. Things generally happen for a reason. That means something caused them to happen. In the case of earths natural cooling/heating cycles the causes tend to be either the output of solar radiation (which isn't changing that much currently), or the position of landmasses and their effect on ocean currents.

Lets look into the landmasses since the output of solar radiation isn't changing that much (it's actually been in decline for the last few years which is indicative of cooling, but it's not changed by much).

If you look at a world map you will see a continuous, uninterrupted circle of water around Antarctica. Also, you'll notice that Antarctica is on the bottom part of the map (top if you have an Australian map). The earth is roughly spherical, and it is spinning. Water acts like a liquid. When you put all of these things together what you end up with is an ocean current that circles Antarctica, all the way around, and doesn't deviate that far to the north. Basically this current, called the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, acts as a heat exchanger (like the radiator in your car). There are two large currents to the north, one in the Pacific Ocean, and one in the Atlantic Ocean. These currents carry warm water from the north down to the Antarctic Circumpolar Current where the ACC cools down the warm water. Since the ACC stays in the south it stays cool year round, and we have a net loss of energy (heat) from the system. Basically when you put warm water somewhere cold (like a refrigerator or freezer), it cools down. Meaning the temperature drops. Look at the position of continents during thermal maximums. They tend to be in supercontinent formations. They are large uninterrupted landmasses that break up ocean currents.
